nine_step_loop.question: What outcome or quality actually matters?
Who is this, in what context?
nine_step_loop.produces: Training age, maturation, capacity, history, schedule, availability
nine_step_loop.common_failure: A program built for a category, not a person

nine_step_loop.question: What quality, and why this one?
nine_step_loop.produces: A named target quality with a rationale
nine_step_loop.common_failure: A method chosen before a target exists

nine_step_loop.question: What method produces the intended stimulus?
nine_step_loop.produces: A method with its intended stimulus stated
nine_step_loop.common_failure: Selection by preference, habit, or equipment

nine_step_loop.question: Enough to adapt, without assuming more is better
nine_step_loop.common_failure: A number imported from somewhere else

nine_step_loop.question: Does this fit the athlete's whole life?
nine_step_loop.produces: Sport, school, sleep, and schedule accounted for
nine_step_loop.common_failure: The program that only works in the gym

nine_step_loop.question: What changed, in what construct, against what baseline?
nine_step_loop.produces: A labeled result with its protocol
nine_step_loop.common_failure: Soreness and fatigue used as proxies

nine_step_loop.question: Did the target outcome change, or only the exercise?
nine_step_loop.produces: A transfer statement, or an honest "not yet established"

nine_step_loop.question: Progress, maintain, regress, redistribute, or change — why?
nine_step_loop.produces: A logged decision with a stated reason
nine_step_loop.common_failure: Change on novelty; no record of reasoning

integrity_rules: The target is named before the method. No exposure is recorded in NovaKore without the target quality it serves (AS-101-01, §21.4).

No stage produces a score. No tool, dashboard, or NovaKore feature may generate a readiness prescription, ACWR injury alert, asymmetry alert, movement-screen injury classification, youth age gate, recovery clock, periodization prescription, or "nonresponder" classification (§21.4).
Transfer is a separate step for a reason. A coach who reports exercise improvement as transfer has skipped step 8.
Adjustment carries a reason. An adjustment without a logged reason is not a decision; it is a preference.

controlled_terminology.definition: Multifactorial sport performance involving technical, tactical, perceptual-cognitive, physical, psychological, and contextual contributors. Physical capacity supports performance but is not equivalent to competitive success.
controlled_terminology.error_prevented: Treating a physical test result as a performance verdict

controlled_terminology.definition: Planned development of physical capacities intended to support athlete health, availability, and performance. An applied umbrella term, not a tightly standardized scientific construct.
controlled_terminology.error_prevented: Arguing about a definition as though it were empirical

controlled_terminology.definition: Chronic change resulting from repeated exposure. Acute response does not equal chronic adaptation.
controlled_terminology.error_prevented: Reading one session as evidence of change

controlled_terminology.definition: Training demand sufficient relative to current capacity and intended adaptation. May be manipulated through load, volume, frequency, density, range of motion, velocity/intent, complexity, technical demand, or exposure distribution.
Purposeful evolution of training demand when justified by target, athlete response, and context. Not synonymous with adding weight.
Adaptation reflects the characteristics of the task performed — force, velocity, contraction mode, ROM, timing, coordination, energetic demand, and skill requirements.
Observed carryover from training to a defined target outcome. Improvement in the trained exercise is not automatically transfer.
controlled_terminology.error_prevented: Reporting exercise improvement as sport improvement

controlled_terminology.definition: Adjustment of training based on meaningful athlete-specific variables and response — not customization for its own sake.
Purposeful change in training variables. Novelty is not itself a training objective.
Temporary reduction in performance or capacity arising from training or other stressors. Fatigue is not evidence of session quality.
Restoration processes that influence subsequent capacity and adaptation. Cannot be reduced to one score or a fixed clock.
A contextual estimate of current ability to perform or tolerate a planned demand. Not a directly measurable single biological state.
controlled_terminology.error_prevented: A dashboard number treated as a state

controlled_terminology.definition: External work performed and/or the internal response to that work. Neither alone represents total adaptation or injury risk.
controlled_terminology.error_prevented: One load metric standing in for the whole

controlled_terminology.definition: History of structured exposure and competency, distinct from chronological age.
controlled_terminology.error_prevented: Age used as a readiness criterion

controlled_terminology.definition: Integration of best available evidence, coaching expertise, athlete characteristics and preferences, and environmental constraints.
controlled_terminology.error_prevented: "The research says," used to end a conversation

doctrine.title: Principles Are Decision Frameworks
doctrine.statement: Training principles guide reasoning. They are not universal algorithms and not rigid biological laws.
doctrine.evidence_note: A/B — Known-Probable. The Evidence Pack's central organizing conclusion is that adaptation, overload, specificity, individualization, variation, fatigue/recovery, transfer, and concurrent-training effects are best treated as conditional decision frameworks rather than universal laws or precise algorithms. Training response depends on the imposed stimulus, athlete history and maturation, sport demands, exposure consistency, recovery context, measurement quality, and the outcome assessed. [EP101-04, EP101-05, EP101-07, EP101-08]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: "Conditional" does not mean "optional" or "anything goes." A principle that is conditional still constrains: it tells the coach what to look at and what would count as evidence. A coach who uses conditionality as a licence to do whatever they prefer has misunderstood the doctrine more badly than one who treats it as a law.

doctrine.title: Adaptation Requires Repeated Relevant Exposure
doctrine.statement: A single session produces responses. Chronic adaptation requires repeated, relevant, appropriately dosed exposure over time. Coaches evaluate trends rather than inferring adaptation from one workout.
doctrine.evidence_note: A — Known for the stimulus-response-adaptation concept; F for the claim that exact adaptation timelines and the optimal next exposure are individually predictable with the precision simplified supercompensation curves imply. The repeated-bout effect means a familiar bout produces less damage and soreness after prior exposure — so reduced soreness does not establish that a program has stopped working. [EP101-04, EP101-05]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Trend-reading is not an excuse for never evaluating. A coach who says "it's a trend, give it time" for six months without a defined outcome or review point has not applied the doctrine — they have avoided measurement.

doctrine.title: Overload Is Multi-Variable
doctrine.statement: Progressive overload means progressively appropriate training demand relative to current capacity and intended adaptation. It is not synonymous with adding external weight.
doctrine.evidence_note: A — Known. Resistance-training variables influence strength and hypertrophy responses, and load, volume, frequency, density, range of motion, contraction emphasis, velocity and intent, exercise complexity, technical demand, and exposure distribution can all change task demand. F for "progressive overload means add weight every session," which is too narrow and can be unsafe or counterproductive when technical, fatigue, or schedule constraints are limiting. [EP101-05, EP101-21, EP101-22]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Rejecting load-only progression is not rejecting load. Load remains one of the most reliable and most easily coached progression variables. The doctrine forbids the reduction, not the tool.

doctrine.title: Progression Must Serve the Target
doctrine.statement: Load, volume, frequency, density, range, velocity or intent, complexity, specificity, or exposure distribution may progress. The variable selected must match the athlete and the intended adaptation.
doctrine.evidence_note: B — Probable that training demand should evolve when justified by target, response, and context; D — Applied coaching inference for the selection of which variable progresses first; F for any universal progression sequence — no evidence supports one. [EP101-05, EP101-07, EP101-21]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: "It depends" is not the answer. The coach must name the variable, name the target it serves, and name what would make them choose differently. A progression decision without a stated target is not individualization; it is improvisation.
doctrine.summary_class: B / D / F on universal sequence

doctrine.title: Specificity Is Multidimensional
doctrine.statement: Specificity is determined by relevant task demands — force, velocity, contraction mode, range, coordination, energetic demand, timing, and skill characteristics — not by how closely an exercise visually resembles the sport.
doctrine.evidence_note: A — Known. Adaptations are shaped by the characteristics of the task performed, and training a target quality tends to improve that quality more directly than unrelated work. F for "an exercise looks like the sport, therefore it transfers better" — visual resemblance alone cannot establish positive transfer, and may reduce loadability, alter coordination, or displace sport practice without proving benefit. [EP101-03, EP101-04]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Rejecting resemblance is not rejecting relevance. A method can be highly specific in the dimensions that matter and look nothing like the sport; another can look identical and be specific in none of them. The question is always specific in which dimension, to which demand.

doctrine.title: Transfer Must Be Evaluated
doctrine.statement: Improvement in an exercise, a test, or a physical quality does not automatically prove improvement in sport performance. Transfer is assessed at a defined target.
doctrine.evidence_class: A for the specificity principle underlying transfer; C to D
doctrine.evidence_note: A for the specificity principle underlying transfer; C to D — Conditional for predicting transfer from a single exercise. Positive, negative, and neutral transfer are all real outcomes. Stronger transfer claims require a clearly described intervention, valid target testing, a relevant comparison, sufficient exposure, and a meaningful outcome beyond the trained task — and sport-performance claims need especially careful interpretation because technical and tactical context, opponent, team system, and competition noise are large confounders. [EP101-03, EP101-04, EP101-30]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Demanding transfer evidence is not demanding a controlled trial before every squat. It is demanding that the coach state the target and the evaluation in advance, and report honestly when transfer has not been established rather than assuming it.

doctrine.title: Physical Preparation Supports Sport; It Does Not Replace Sport
doctrine.statement: Performance training develops physical capacities. Sport practice develops sport-specific skill, perception, decision-making, and tactical execution. The two are not substitutes.
doctrine.evidence_note: A — Known that physical training can improve component qualities such as strength, hypertrophy, sprint, jump, and power outcomes within studied populations; B — Probable that improvements in component qualities may contribute to sport performance, with the practical effect sport-, athlete-, and task-dependent. Direct sport-performance transfer must be demonstrated rather than inferred from mechanics. [EP101-03, EP101-04, EP101-13, EP101-25, EP101-26]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: This is not a demotion of the weight room. A method can be valuable even when it does not resemble a sport action, provided it develops a limiting or target quality that contributes in the athlete's context. The doctrine sets the claim boundary, not the value.

doctrine.title: Individualization Begins With Meaningful Differences
doctrine.statement: Training age, maturation, current capacity, sport demand, schedule, history, availability, and response matter. Individualization does not require unnecessary complexity.
doctrine.evidence_note: A — Known that athletes differ in baseline status, maturation, training age, strength level, schedule, injury history, sport demands, and recovery context, and that these alter both tolerance and response; B — Supported practice that individualization should begin with known, decision-relevant variables rather than bespoke programming of every variable for every athlete; D for athlete preference and adherence influencing selection where multiple methods are similarly appropriate. [EP101-01, EP101-04, EP101-11, EP101-14]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Individualization is not the same as customization. Twelve different programs for twelve athletes who share a demand, a schedule, and a training age is not individualization — it is a coaching load the environment cannot sustain, and it makes evaluation impossible.

doctrine.title: Variation Must Have a Reason
doctrine.statement: Variation is useful when it solves a programming problem, changes an intended stimulus, manages fatigue, or addresses changing demands. Novelty for its own sake is not a training principle.
doctrine.evidence_note: B — Probable that planned variation can be useful, particularly for strength-oriented programming and logistical management: volume-equated synthesis found periodized training had an advantage for maximal strength over non-periodized training, while hypertrophy superiority was not clearly established and linear versus undulating approaches showed no consistent difference. D for keeping a structure stable long enough to coach, load, and evaluate it. F for "muscle confusion," constant rotation, and novelty as goals. [EP101-05, EP101-07]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Two findings are held together and neither is dropped: planned variation beats no plan for strength, and no named model beats another. A coach who cites the first to justify a branded system has used half the evidence.

doctrine.title: Fatigue Is a Cost, Not the Product
doctrine.statement: Fatigue and soreness may accompany training but do not establish effectiveness. Training quality is judged against intended adaptation and performance outcomes.
doctrine.evidence_note: A — Known that fatigue is a reduction in capacity that can occur alongside productive training; F for soreness or fatigue as proof of session quality — soreness can occur with novel or eccentric work but does not quantify adaptation. Absence of fatigue is likewise not proof of failure. [EP101-04, EP101-05, EP101-10, EP101-15, EP101-19]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: The correction does not make fatigue meaningless. Fatigue is real information about exposure and tolerance, and managing it is a coaching obligation (obligation 6). What it is not is a measure of whether the session worked.

doctrine.title: Recovery Is Contextual
doctrine.statement: Recovery depends on the athlete, the exposure, sport demands, sleep, nutrition, psychological stress, and time. No universal 48- or 72-hour rule and no supercompensation timetable governs all athletes.
doctrine.evidence_note: A — Known that sleep, nutritional adequacy, psychological stress, sport demands, and training load influence recovery and performance context; B — Supported practice for using multiple signals to make proportionate adjustments; F for the claim that soreness, fatigue, a fixed 48/72-hour rule, or a readiness score can precisely determine when a specific athlete is fully recovered. [EP101-04, EP101-10, EP101-15, EP101-19]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Rejecting the fixed clock does not mean scheduling is arbitrary. A G3 coach still plans spacing deliberately — they simply plan it from demand, schedule, and observed response rather than from a number they were told.
doctrine.summary_class: A / B / F on fixed rules

doctrine.title: Dose Is Outcome- and Context-Specific
doctrine.statement: More training is not automatically better. Effective dose balances adaptation opportunity against fatigue, adherence, schedule, and recoverability.
doctrine.evidence_note: A — Known that in healthy adults volume is associated with strength and hypertrophy outcomes with likely diminishing returns as dose rises, the exact curve differing by outcome and design; B — Probable that lower doses can improve performance, especially in novices or when a quality is maintained rather than maximized; D for "minimum effective dose" and "maximum recoverable volume" as communication heuristics; F for presenting either as a precisely discoverable individual constant. Unknown for exact individualized thresholds. [EP101-04, EP101-05, EP101-21, EP101-22, EP101-29]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Rejecting "more is better" is not adopting "less is better." Dose is a judgment about opportunity and cost, made against a target — and a coach who systematically under-doses because dosing feels risky has made the opposite error with the same root.

doctrine.title: Concurrent Training Is Manageable
doctrine.statement: Strength, power, and endurance can coexist. Interference is conditional and must be managed rather than treated as universal incompatibility.
doctrine.evidence_note: A/B — Known-Probable that strength and endurance can be developed concurrently and that blanket exclusion of conditioning is unsupported; B — Probable that interference becomes practically meaningful when high endurance volume coexists with strength or power priorities, when sessions are closely coupled, when running and impact demand is high, or when fatigue management is poor. A systematic review reported small interference for lower-body strength in males but not females, varying by training status; other meta-analytic evidence suggests explosive strength/power and fiber hypertrophy may be more vulnerable than maximal strength, with running potentially more problematic than cycling for some outcomes. F for "cardio kills gains." Exact thresholds are not universal. [EP101-08, EP101-09, EP101-31]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: "Manageable" is not "ignorable." The doctrine rejects the prohibition, not the phenomenon. A coach who stacks a heavy running block against a power priority and cites this doctrine has inverted it.

doctrine.title: Training Age and Maturation Outrank Arbitrary Age Rules
doctrine.statement: Chronological age alone does not determine readiness for resistance, speed, plyometric, or power training.
doctrine.evidence_note: B — Supported practice. Training age is exposure and competency history, not chronological age; biological maturation and prior training can be more decision-relevant than age alone, especially in youth. Novice/intermediate/advanced labels are useful shorthand, but no universal evidence-based cut points classify every athlete. [EP101-11, EP101-12, EP101-13]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Rejecting age gates does not make age irrelevant. Chronological age carries real information about maturation, schooling, supervision context, and psychological readiness — it simply is not a sufficient criterion on its own.

doctrine.title: Youth Can Train
doctrine.statement: Properly supervised and developmentally appropriate youth resistance, speed, plyometric, and power training are legitimate components of athletic development.
doctrine.evidence_note: A — Known that position statements and systematic reviews support youth resistance training when qualified instruction, supervision, sensible progression, and appropriate technique are present; B — Probable that youth can train strength, power, sprinting, and plyometric qualities when task demands are scaled to competency and context, with adolescent meta-analyses reporting improvements in jump, sprint, COD, and explosive-strength outcomes. F for: lifting stunts growth; a specific age must be reached first; youth should only use bodyweight; youth cannot train power; puberty must occur before meaningful physical preparation. [EP101-11, EP101-12, EP101-13, EP101-25, EP101-26]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: These findings do not justify unsupervised lifting, arbitrary heavy loading, adult-style volume, or progression beyond technical and psychological readiness. The research is more robust for supervised interventions than for unsupervised real-world implementation. Samples are frequently adolescent and male-dominant rather than prepubertal or female.

doctrine.title: Technique Is Task- and Athlete-Constrained
doctrine.statement: Coaches require safe and effective technical standards, but one universal movement solution does not fit every athlete or task.
doctrine.evidence_note: B — Supported practice that coaches should establish task-relevant setup, intent, execution constraints, and progression criteria, using demonstration, concise cues, and feedback appropriate to athlete and task; augmented feedback can improve motor learning and acute resistance-training performance, with effectiveness depending on form, timing, frequency, and context — constant immediate correction is not automatically optimal. F for a universal movement-screen score, one asymmetry threshold, or one technique template predicting injury or dictating a single correct solution for every athlete. [EP101-01, EP101-20, EP101-23, EP101-24]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Movement variability is not a licence for uncoached movement. Anthropometry, history, task goal, equipment, and coordination produce legitimate variation within task-relevant constraints the coach still defines and still enforces.

doctrine.title: Monitoring Informs; It Does Not Diagnose
doctrine.statement: Load, wellness, readiness, heart rate, GPS, RPE, movement screens, asymmetry, and ACWR can contribute information. None independently determines injury, recovery, adaptation, or prescription.
doctrine.evidence_note: B — Supported practice that monitoring supports a multifactorial decision process; C — Conditional that athlete-reported measures relate to subsequent performance or load, with variable relationships that do not support deterministic prescription from a single score; F for a readiness score automatically determining today's training, for ACWR as a precise injury predictor with a fixed safe zone, and for movement-screen composites as standalone injury prediction. [EP101-15, EP101-16, EP101-18, EP101-19, EP101-32, EP101-33, EP101-35, EP101-36, EP101-37]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: "Does not diagnose" is not "do not collect." A coach who abandons monitoring because it cannot diagnose has replaced false precision with no information. The standard is triangulation (AS-101-07), not abstinence.
doctrine.summary_class: B / C / F on standalone use

doctrine.title: Testing Must Earn Interpretation
doctrine.statement: A measurement must be sufficiently valid, reliable, standardized, and relevant before it should influence a coaching decision.
doctrine.evidence_note: A — Known that a test can be valid for one construct and not another, that a reliable test is required to detect small meaningful change, and that standardized protocols and familiarization reduce avoidable noise; B — Supported practice for preferring repeated within-athlete baselines and context-consistent testing over uncritical normative comparison; C — Conditional for smallest worthwhile change, which is conceptually useful but whose calculation and practical threshold depend on context, test reliability, and decision use — it is not a universal cut point. [EP101-38, EP101-39]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: The bar is proportional to the decision. A coach does not need laboratory reliability to decide whether to add five pounds; they do need it before telling an athlete a quality has changed. Match the rigor to the consequence.

doctrine.title: Technology Does Not Create Validity
doctrine.statement: Technology can improve data acquisition. It cannot rescue an invalid question, an unreliable measure, a poor protocol, or an unsupported interpretation.
doctrine.evidence_class: F for "technology makes programming more scientific"
doctrine.evidence_note: F for "technology makes programming more scientific" — technology can improve measurement, but validity, reliability, context, and interpretation still govern use. Session RPE, GPS and wearables, heart rate, and wellness questionnaires can be useful monitoring inputs when measurement is standardized and interpreted alongside context; they are not direct measures of tissue state, adaptation, or injury causation. [EP101-18, EP101-38]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: This is not technology scepticism. A device that answers a question the coach had already formed is worth having. The doctrine simply denies that the device supplies the question, the protocol, or the meaning.

doctrine.title: Evidence Sets Boundaries; Coaching Judgment Operates Within Them
doctrine.statement: Research evidence, coaching expertise, athlete context, and operational constraints must be integrated, without allowing either research slogans or personal experience to override stronger evidence.
doctrine.evidence_note: B — Supported practice. Evidence-based practice integrates best available research with coach expertise, athlete values and preferences, and environmental constraints. It is neither "research says, therefore everyone must" nor "experience overrides research." Survey evidence indicates practitioners, coaches, and athletes value research-informed practice while also valuing sport knowledge, experience, and communication — perception evidence, not evidence that any individual practice is effective. [EP101-01, EP101-02, EP101-40]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: The integration is not a 50/50 split, and it is not permission to overrule strong evidence with a strong feeling. Judgment operates within the boundary the evidence sets — and the coach must be able to say where that boundary is (§21.3).

doctrine.title: Scope of Practice Is Part of Coaching Competence
doctrine.statement: Performance coaches train and monitor performance. They do not independently diagnose medical conditions, provide medical clearance, or substitute for qualified healthcare professionals.
doctrine.evidence_note: A/B — Known-Probable. Performance coaches should manage training exposure, technique, progressions, observation, and communication, and should not diagnose, independently clear return to sport, prescribe rehabilitation beyond scope, or substitute for athletic trainers, physicians, physical therapists, psychologists, or dietitians when indicated. Functional overreaching, nonfunctional overreaching, and overtraining syndrome are not interchangeable; OTS requires broader assessment and exclusion of other conditions and is unsuitable for casual coach diagnosis. [EP101-10, EP101-11, EP101-12]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Scope is a competence, not a disclaimer. Recognizing the boundary early, communicating clearly, and referring well is skilled coaching — not an admission of limitation. Referring reflexively to avoid a conversation is its own failure.

applied_standards.title: Define the Target Before the Method
applied_standards.statement: Name the desired performance quality or outcome before selecting exercises or technology.
applied_standards.enforcement: every exposure object requires target_quality and demand (§21.4).
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Separate Acute Response From Chronic Adaptation
applied_standards.statement: Do not use soreness, fatigue, pump, sweat, or a single performance response as proof of adaptation.
applied_standards.boundary: acute information is still information — it is evidence about exposure and tolerance, not about adaptation.
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Progress the Variable That Solves the Problem
applied_standards.statement: Do not default to load progression when another variable better serves the target.
applied_standards.evidence_basis: D — applied inference from multi-variable overload (D101-03, D101-04).
applied_standards.boundary: no universal progression sequence is published (CJ-19).
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Require a Transfer Rationale
applied_standards.statement: For every major method, state what it is expected to improve and how that improvement will be evaluated.
applied_standards.evidence_basis: A/C — the specificity principle is A; transfer prediction from a single exercise is C–D (D101-06).
applied_standards.enforcement: every exposure object requires transfer_rationale and evaluation_method (§21.4).
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Preserve Program Stability Long Enough to Coach and Evaluate
applied_standards.statement: Do not rotate exercises solely to create novelty. Change when demand, response, constraints, or practical utility justify it.
applied_standards.boundary: no minimum block length is published. Stability long enough to coach, load, and evaluate is a judgment (CJ-19).
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Individualize From Known Variables First
applied_standards.statement: Prioritize training age, maturation, current capacity, technical competency, schedule, sport exposure, injury and training history, and response.
applied_standards.boundary: individualization is not customization; a shared program for athletes who share a demand is a legitimate result.
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Use Multiple Inputs for Readiness Decisions
applied_standards.statement: Combine athlete report, recent exposure, schedule, performance trend, and coach observation when adjustment is necessary.
applied_standards.enforcement: readiness_decision requires at least three distinct input types (§21.4).
applied_standards.standing: the three-input minimum is a G3 Applied Standard, not a research finding.
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: No Single Metric Governs Training
applied_standards.statement: No ACWR value, movement-screen score, asymmetry percentage, wellness score, or readiness value independently dictates programming.
applied_standards.standing: binding prohibition — enforced in the data layer (§21.4).
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Standardize Before Comparing
applied_standards.statement: Testing requires consistent protocol, equipment, instructions, warm-up, familiarization, and calculation.
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Interpret Change Against Measurement Error
applied_standards.statement: Do not treat small test changes as real without considering reliability, typical error, baseline variability, and decision consequences.
applied_standards.evidence_basis: A/C — the principle is A; smallest worthwhile change as a calculation is C (D101-18).
applied_standards.boundary: no universal cut point is published — the threshold depends on the test and the decision.
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Youth Progress by Competence and Exposure
applied_standards.statement: Use supervision, technique, training age, maturity, psychological readiness, and task demand rather than unsupported age prohibitions.
applied_standards.enforcement: supervision ratio documented for every youth group.
applied_standards.boundary: competence-based progression is not a licence for adult dosing (§18.1).
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Manage Concurrent Demands
applied_standards.statement: Account for endurance, strength, speed, power, sport practice, competition, and recovery rather than treating conditioning as categorically harmful.
applied_standards.boundary: no separation interval, sequence, or modality rule is published (CJ-08).
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Technique Standards Must Be Purposeful
applied_standards.statement: Coach task-relevant positions, intent, execution, and safety constraints while allowing legitimate athlete-specific movement solutions.
applied_standards.boundary: no universal movement template is published (CJ-20), and no template may be inferred from an example.
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Use Technology Only for an Actionable Question
applied_standards.statement: Do not collect a metric unless its meaning, reliability, and the possible coaching response are understood before collection.
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Refer Beyond Scope
applied_standards.statement: Escalate medical, injury, nutritional, psychological, or return-to-play concerns to qualified professionals when appropriate.
applied_standards.boundary: referral is not avoidance — the coach still communicates, documents, and adapts training within scope.
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Disclose Population Transfer
applied_standards.statement: Any claim extended beyond the population in which it was established carries an explicit disclosure at the point of the claim.
applied_standards.evidence_basis: A — the Evidence Pack's population-transfer limitations are explicit and extensive (§18.3).
applied_standards.enforcement: every module evidence block carries a population-transfer line; a module object without one fails production validation (§21.5).
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

coach_judgment.evidence_position: Volume relates to strength and hypertrophy outcomes with diminishing returns; exact curve differs by outcome and design

claim_audit.g3_teaches: Pain is not a required marker of productive adaptation and may signal injury or inappropriate loading. Discomfort and pain are not the same thing, and the coach must be able to distinguish them. D101-10, §19. [EP101-10]

Soreness can occur with novel or eccentric work but does not quantify adaptation or session quality. Adaptation is read from a trend on a defined outcome. D101-02, D101-10, AS-101-02. [EP101-04, EP101-05]
Dose-response includes diminishing returns, fatigue cost, and context dependence. Less is not therefore better — dose is a judgment against a target. D101-12. [EP101-21, EP101-29]
Outcome, technique, velocity, volume, and athlete readiness all matter. Load remains a primary tool; it is not the only one and not always the right one. D101-03, D101-04. [EP101-21, EP101-22]
Maintenance, technical practice, recovery, and strategic low-load exposures can be appropriate. A session with a purpose other than overload is not a wasted session. D101-03. [EP101-05]

Multiple variables can progress: load, volume, frequency, density, ROM, contraction emphasis, velocity and intent, complexity, technical demand, exposure distribution. The variable must serve the target. D101-03, D101-04, AS-101-03. [EP101-05, EP101-21]

claim_audit.claim: Sport-specific exercises should resemble the sport
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Specificity is multidimensional. Resemblance is not proof of transfer and may reduce loadability, alter coordination, or displace sport practice. Name the dimension. D101-05, D101-06. [EP101-03]

claim_audit.claim: Unstable-surface training is automatically more sport-specific
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Visual and contextual similarity does not establish transfer, and instability may reduce force expression. The method is not thereby useless — it is simply not sport-specific by virtue of instability. D101-05. [EP101-03]

claim_audit.claim: Every athlete needs identical movement standards
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Task-relevant standards matter, and individual solutions legitimately vary with anthropometry, history, goal, equipment, and coordination. Constraints, not templates. D101-16, AS-101-13. [EP101-01, EP101-23]

claim_audit.claim: Cardio kills strength and muscle gains
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Concurrent training can develop both. Interference is conditional on outcome, modality, dose, training status, sequencing, proximity, and recovery — and it is not zero. D101-13, AS-101-12. [EP101-08, EP101-09, EP101-31]
Supervised youth resistance training is supported and no fixed-age ban is justified. D101-15, AS-101-11. [EP101-11, EP101-12]

Load decisions require supervision, competency, progression, and context. An arbitrary blanket prohibition is unsupported — and so is arbitrary heavy loading. Both fail. D101-15, CJ-18. [EP101-11, EP101-12]

claim_audit.claim: Youth should not perform power training
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Appropriately supervised plyometric and power training can improve youth outcomes. Scaled to competency and context. D101-15. [EP101-25, EP101-26]

claim_audit.claim: Athletes must specialize early to become elite
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Sport-specific and developmental context matter; the blanket claim exceeds the evidence. The opposite blanket claim — that multisport participation is always superior — also exceeds it. CJ-21. [EP101-11, EP101-12]
Purposeful variation can help; novelty alone is not a mechanism. Variation must solve a problem. D101-09, AS-101-05. [EP101-05, EP101-07]
No credible scientific construct supports the claim. The correction is not "never change anything" — it is "change for a reason." D101-09. [EP101-05]
Recovery varies by task, athlete, exposure, and context. No replacement window is published. D101-11, CJ-04. [EP101-04, EP101-15]

claim_audit.claim: Supercompensation tells you exactly when to train again
claim_audit.g3_teaches: A useful heuristic for explaining that training creates both adaptation and fatigue — not an individual biological timetable. Class E (§17.4). D101-11. [EP101-04, EP101-05]

claim_audit.claim: Fatigue means the session was productive
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Fatigue can be expected, excessive, or unrelated to the desired adaptation. It is a cost, not the product — and its absence is not failure. D101-10. [EP101-10, EP101-15]
No foundational evidence supports failure as a universal requirement; dose and task context matter. Failure may be used deliberately where its cost is justified. D101-12. [EP101-21, EP101-22]
Planned variation can help — the formality and the model depend on context. This entry is a boundary, not a plain F: the claim is over-stated, not false. D101-09, CJ-07. [EP101-07]

claim_audit.claim: One periodization model is universally superior
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Linear versus undulating superiority is not consistently established. Organize deliberately; call the organization an Organizational Choice. D101-09, §17.4. [EP101-07]

Screening evidence is inconsistent or insufficient for injury prediction. A screen describes task performance under a protocol. Describing is still useful. D101-16, §19.2. [EP101-32, EP101-33, EP101-34]
Asymmetry requires task and context interpretation; no universal predictive threshold is established. No replacement threshold is published. §19.3, AS-101-08. [EP101-32, EP101-33]
Associations exist in some datasets, but calculation heterogeneity and statistical concerns prevent standalone prediction. One contextual input. §19.5, CJ-13. [EP101-35, EP101-36, EP101-37]

claim_audit.claim: A readiness score automatically determines today's training
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Multidimensional trends and context are required. A score is one input among at least three (AS-101-07). D101-17. [EP101-15, EP101-19]
Technology can improve measurement, but validity, reliability, context, and interpretation still govern use. A device does not supply the question. D101-19, AS-101-14. [EP101-18, EP101-38]

claim_audit.claim: A poor response to one metric after one block proves a biological "nonresponder"
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Apparent nonresponse may be outcome-specific, dose-dependent, adherence-dependent, measurement-dependent, or temporary; broad global nonresponse is unlikely on current conceptual analysis. Run the five checks (§10.10). D101-08. [EP101-27, EP101-28]

claim_audit_symmetry_rule: Every correction is a correction, not an inversion. Correct overstatement without creating the opposite absolute. Inverting an audited claim fails competency C101-18 from the other side and is scored as a failure.

modules.title: What Athletic Performance Training Is
modules.framing_statement: Most coaching arguments are definitional arguments that nobody has noticed are definitional. This module removes four of them before they can cost an athlete anything.
modules.purpose: To establish what athletic performance is, what physical preparation can and cannot do, and what the performance coach is actually responsible for — so that every later decision has a defined subject.

learning_objectives.objective: Define athletic performance as multifactorial, and name its contributors.
Distinguish physical capacity, sport skill, and competitive performance.
Define physical preparation as an applied umbrella term rather than a fixed scientific construct.
State what the GPP / SPP / sport-specific / sport-practice taxonomy is and is not.
Explain why a method can be valuable without resembling the sport.
State the boundary of the performance coach's role.

evidence_classifications.statement: Sport performance is determined by technical, tactical, perceptual-cognitive, physical, psychological, and contextual factors
Physical capacity can support sport performance but is not equivalent to sport skill or competitive success
Physical training can improve component qualities — strength, hypertrophy, sprint, jump, power — within studied populations
Improvements in component qualities may contribute to sport performance; the practical effect is sport-, athlete-, and task-dependent
Physical preparation and strength and conditioning are practical umbrella terms, not tightly standardized scientific constructs
GPP / SPP / sport-specific / sport-practice labels are useful coaching language, not a complete causal model of transfer
Training principles are conditional decision frameworks rather than universal laws
A method can be valuable without visual sport resemblance if it develops a limiting or target quality

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: the definitional material is conceptual rather than population-limited. The component-quality evidence is drawn substantially from adults and from male-dominant samples, and the youth outcome evidence is adolescent-weighted — disclosed again wherever it is used to justify a method (M4, M9).
modules.coach_judgment: whether the GPP/SPP taxonomy is used in a given conversation, and how emphasis is distributed across it (CJ-10).

lessons.title: Four arguments that are really definitions
lessons.content: "Is that sport-specific?" · "Is conditioning training?" · "Does the weight room make athletes better?" · "Is he a good athlete?" Each is unanswerable until the terms are fixed.

lessons.title: Athletic performance, defined
lessons.content: The six contributor families, and why physical capacity is one of them rather than the whole.

lessons.title: What physical preparation is for
lessons.content: Health, availability, and performance support — with availability named explicitly, because it is the contribution coaches most often fail to claim.

lessons.title: Capacity, skill, and performance
lessons.content: Three different things that improve at different rates, respond to different work, and are measured differently.

lessons.title: GPP, SPP, and honest labeling
lessons.content: The taxonomy as adopted G3 language (§3.3), its three constraints, and the sentence that marks it as language rather than science.

lessons.title: Why resemblance is not the test
lessons.content: Introduced here, developed fully in M4: a method earns its place by developing a limiting or target quality, not by looking like the game.

lessons.title: The role and its edges
lessons.content: What a performance coach does, and the first statement of scope (D101-21) that M12 completes.

modules.coaching_applications: Applied immediately to how G3 sessions and blocks are labeled. "Speed day" is a schedule entry, not a target. The module ends with coaches rewriting their own current session labels into demand-and-target language.

common_errors_claim_audit.text: Treating a physical test result as a performance verdict · using "sport-specific" as a property an exercise owns (CA-07) · defending a definition as though it were a finding · claiming sport outcomes for weight-room work (CA-07 family, developed in M4) · describing the coach's role in terms that overlap medical scope (D101-21).

modules.case_scenario: Scenario M1-A — Four labels, one athlete. A high-school athlete's week is presented as it is actually labeled — "speed," "lift," "conditioning," "skills." Coaches rewrite each block as demand, target quality, and intended contribution, then identify which of the four they cannot rewrite without more information.

modules.title: Adaptation: What Training Actually Changes
modules.framing_statement: A coach who cannot tell a response from an adaptation will spend a career reacting to noise — changing programs that were working and keeping ones that were not.
modules.purpose: To install the acute-versus-chronic distinction, the trend-reading habit that follows from it, and the specific reason that soreness cannot be used as a readout.

learning_objectives.objective: Distinguish acute response from chronic adaptation.
Explain why repeated, relevant, tolerable exposure is required for adaptation.
Explain the repeated-bout effect and its consequence for program judgment.
Explain why exact adaptation timing is not individually predictable from field models.
Identify what a single session can and cannot establish.
Describe how a trend is evaluated: what is measured, over what period, against what.
State why "nonresponder" is a claim requiring caution.

evidence_classifications.statement: Training produces acute responses; repeated appropriately dosed exposure can produce chronic adaptation
Exact adaptation timelines and the optimal next exposure are not individually predictable with the precision simplified supercompensation curves imply
evidence_classifications.class: F / Known against the precision claim

evidence_classifications.statement: The repeated-bout effect means a familiar bout produces less damage and soreness after prior exposure
Reduced soreness does not establish that a program has become ineffective or that exercises must be changed
Training status, prior exposure, adherence, outcome choice, measurement error, and recovery context all modify observed response
Apparent nonresponse may be outcome-specific, dose-dependent, measurement-dependent, or temporary; broad global nonresponse is unlikely on current conceptual analysis
Soreness quantifies adaptation or session quality

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: the adaptation and repeated-bout literature is adult-weighted and not youth-specific; the responder/nonresponder analysis is conceptual and not resistance-training-exclusive. Both are disclosed where the material is applied to youth (M9).
modules.coach_judgment: how long a trend must run before it is read (CJ-05, CJ-19); which outcome is the one worth tracking for this athlete.

lessons.title: Two timescales
lessons.content: What happens in a session, what happens across a block, and why coaches routinely read the first as evidence of the second.

lessons.title: What adaptation requires
lessons.content: Repeated · relevant · tolerable · sustained. Remove any one and the exposure stops producing change.

lessons.title: The repeated-bout effect
lessons.content: Why the third week feels easier, and why that is the program working rather than the program failing.

lessons.title: The supercompensation problem
lessons.content: A useful picture with a false promise: it explains a relationship, it does not schedule an athlete. Full historical treatment in M6.

lessons.title: Reading a trend
lessons.content: What is measured, how often, over what period, against what baseline — and what would count as no change.

lessons.title: Variability and its sources
lessons.content: Training status, adherence, outcome selection, measurement error, recovery context. Each is checked before biology is blamed.

lessons.title: "Nonresponder," carefully
lessons.content: What the label would require, why it is almost never available after one block, and what to say instead (§3.2).

modules.coaching_applications: Applied to how G3 evaluates a block. The module produces a standing G3 habit: before changing a program, state which of the five variability sources has been ruled out.

modules.title: Overload, Progression & Dose
modules.framing_statement: "Progressive overload" is the most-cited and least-understood phrase in the profession. This module replaces it with a question the coach can actually answer: which variable, and why that one?
modules.purpose: To establish overload as multi-variable demand, progression as a targeted choice, and dose as a judgment about opportunity against cost — without publishing a single number G3 cannot support.

learning_objectives.objective: Define overload as demand relative to current capacity and intended adaptation.
Name the variables through which demand can be changed.
Select a progression variable for a stated target and justify the selection.
Explain why no universal progression sequence exists.
Explain dose-response, diminishing returns, and their limits.
Use "minimum effective dose" and "maximum recoverable volume" correctly, as heuristics.
Explain why not every session must create overload.

evidence_classifications.statement: Resistance-training variables influence strength and hypertrophy responses
Volume has a dose-response relationship with hypertrophy within the bounds of the evidence base
Demand can be changed through load, volume, frequency, density, ROM, contraction emphasis, velocity/intent, complexity, technical demand, and exposure distribution
Frequency can facilitate distribution and may support strength gains; its independent effect is often entangled with volume, training status, and task practice
A coach may progress load, volume, complexity, velocity, density, range, or specificity when the change matches target and readiness
No evidence supports one universal progression sequence
Lower doses can improve performance, especially in novices or when maintaining a quality
Diminishing returns are likely as dose rises; the exact curve differs by outcome and design
"Minimum effective dose" and "maximum recoverable volume" as communication heuristics
Exact individualized dose thresholds discoverable without repeated valid measurement
"Progressive overload means add weight every session"
Every session must create overload
evidence_classifications.class: F / Probable against claim — maintenance, technical practice, recovery, and strategic low-load exposures can be appropriate

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: the dose-response and resistance-training-variable evidence is drawn from healthy adults, frequently male or mixed samples. Exact set, frequency, or progression claims may not be transferred to youth without adaptation (§18.1, §18.3). The most recent dose-response meta-regression is flagged for downstream risk-of-bias review before any precise educational claim rests on it (§20.1).
modules.coach_judgment: weekly volume (CJ-01) · frequency (CJ-02) · intensity (CJ-03) · minimum effective dose (CJ-05) · maximum recoverable volume (CJ-06) · exercise order (CJ-09) · progression sequence (CJ-19).

lessons.title: What overload actually means
lessons.content: Demand relative to capacity and target — the definition that makes the rest of the module possible.

lessons.title: Ten ways to change demand
lessons.content: Load, volume, frequency, density, ROM, contraction emphasis, velocity and intent, complexity, technical demand, exposure distribution — each with what it is good for and what it costs.

lessons.title: Choosing the variable
lessons.content: The target selects the variable. Worked examples in which load is the right answer, and worked examples in which it is the expensive answer.

lessons.title: Why there is no sequence
lessons.content: What a universal progression ladder would require, and why the evidence does not supply one.

lessons.title: Dose and diminishing returns
lessons.content: What the volume evidence supports, in whom, for which outcomes — and where the curve stops being knowable.

lessons.title: MED and MRV, honestly
lessons.content: Useful for talking about a real trade-off; not individual constants a coach can discover. The G3 sentence for each.

lessons.title: Sessions that are not supposed to overload
lessons.content: Maintenance, technical practice, deliberate low-load exposure, and the coaching confidence to run them.

modules.coaching_applications: Applied to G3 progression records. From this module on, every progression entered in NovaKore names the variable and the target it serves — the constraint is enforced in the data layer (§21.4).

modules.title: Specificity & Transfer
modules.framing_statement: Specificity is the most abused principle in the profession, because it is the one that can be faked visually. This module makes the coach name the dimension.
modules.purpose: To replace resemblance-based reasoning with dimensional specificity, and to establish transfer as something evaluated at a defined target rather than assumed.

learning_objectives.objective: Define specificity by task demands rather than appearance.
Name the dimensions along which a task can be specific.
Explain why visual resemblance cannot establish transfer.
Define transfer against a stated target outcome.
Distinguish positive, negative, and neutral transfer.
State what stronger transfer evidence requires.
Explain why unstable-surface work is not automatically more sport-specific.

evidence_classifications.statement: Adaptations are shaped by the force, velocity, contraction mode, range, coordination, energetic demand, timing, and skill characteristics of the task performed
Training that practices a target quality tends to improve that quality more directly than unrelated work
Mechanical, velocity, contraction-mode, ROM, and coordination correspondences help reason about likely transfer; relative importance depends on target task and limiting factors
Dynamic correspondence is a useful structured framework for analyzing transfer characteristics
evidence_classifications.class: E / Historical framework — not an experimentally complete law predicting transfer from resemblance

evidence_classifications.statement: Strength gains can transfer to jump or sprint outcomes in some contexts; magnitude depends on training status, baseline strength, program content, testing, and sport practice
Predicting transfer from a single exercise
Stronger transfer claims require a described intervention, valid target testing, a relevant comparison, sufficient exposure, and an outcome beyond the trained task
Sport-performance transfer claims are confounded by technical/tactical context, opponent, team system, and competition noise
"An exercise looks like the sport, therefore it transfers better"
"Unstable-surface training is more sport-specific"
evidence_classifications.class: F / Probable against universal claim — similarity does not establish transfer, and instability may reduce force expression

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: the specificity and transfer analysis rests substantially on narrative and applied review rather than direct experimental proof for every transfer claim, and the elite-athlete sport-performance review spans different sports and interventions. Both limitations are stated at the point of the claim.
modules.coach_judgment: which exercises best serve a target quality in a particular environment; how much transfer evidence is required before a method earns a place in a limited week.

lessons.title: The resemblance trap
lessons.content: Three exercises that look like a sport and are specific in none of the dimensions that matter; two that look nothing like it and are.

lessons.title: The dimensions
lessons.content: Force · velocity · contraction mode · range · coordination · energetic demand · timing · skill. Naming the dimension is the whole skill.

lessons.title: Dynamic correspondence as a checklist
lessons.content: What it contributes, why coaches use it, and the Class E sentence that keeps it honest (§17.4).

lessons.title: Transfer, defined at a target
lessons.content: Exercise performance · physical test · sport-relevant movement · sport performance. Four different endpoints, four different claims.

lessons.title: Positive, negative, neutral
lessons.content: Negative transfer taught explicitly, because coaches rarely consider that a method can cost something.

lessons.title: What a transfer claim requires
lessons.content: The five conditions, and the honest position when they are absent: not yet established.

lessons.title: Unstable surfaces, worked through
lessons.content: A full application of the module: what is claimed, what dimension is actually altered, what is given up.

modules.coaching_applications: Applied to G3 exercise selection. Every method in a G3 program carries a one-line transfer rationale — what it is expected to improve, and how that will be evaluated (AS-101-04). Methods that cannot carry one are not forbidden; they are labeled as general development.

common_errors_claim_audit.text: Sport-looking exercises assumed to transfer (CA-07) · unstable-surface work called sport-specific (CA-08) · exercise improvement reported as sport improvement (§1.2) · "specific" used with no dimension named · a correlation between a quality and a sport outcome read as a training prescription · negative transfer never considered.

knowledge_assessment.item: Specificity is best determined by…
Which are dimensions of specificity?
An athlete's trained lift improved 20% and their sprint did not. What can be concluded?
State the five conditions for a stronger transfer claim.
A program justifies an exercise entirely by resemblance.

applied_assessment.title: Transfer rationale set
applied_assessment.description: For four methods in the coach's own program, a written rationale naming the target, the specific dimension, the expected change, and the evaluation.
applied_assessment.standard: each dimension named explicitly; at least one method honestly labeled "general development, transfer not established"; no resemblance-based justification.

modules.title: Individualization & Athlete Context
modules.framing_statement: Individualization is not the number of different programs on the whiteboard. It is whether the differences that exist are the ones that matter.
modules.purpose: To establish which athlete variables are decision-relevant, why individualization is not customization, and why "nonresponder" is a claim a foundational coach should almost never make.

learning_objectives.objective: Name the athlete variables that alter tolerance and response.
Distinguish individualization from customization.
Explain why a shared program can be a legitimate individualization result.
Explain how measurement reliability, dose, adherence, and outcome choice affect apparent response.
Explain the role of athlete preference and adherence in selection.
State why sex is treated as one potential modifier rather than a deficit assumption.
State what a "nonresponder" claim would require.

evidence_classifications.statement: Athletes differ in baseline status, maturation, training age, strength level, schedule, injury history, sport demands, and recovery context, altering tolerance and response
Individualization should begin with known, decision-relevant variables rather than bespoke programming of every variable
Athlete preference and adherence may legitimately influence selection where multiple methods are similarly appropriate
evidence_classifications.class: D / Applied inference — direct causal evidence less complete than for dose variables
evidence_classifications.basis: EP101-01 — governance record; carried at the class the Evidence Pack assigns, as an inference rather than a finding

evidence_classifications.statement: Estimates of "true responders" are sensitive to measurement reliability, repeated exposure, outcome selection, adherence, and statistical design
Relative hypertrophy and lower-body strength adaptations are broadly similar under equivalent resistance training across sexes; fatigue characteristics and specific outcomes may differ
One female-specific programming rule applies to all women athletes
A single poor response to one metric after one block proves a biological "nonresponder"

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: sex-differences evidence varies by training history and does not represent female athletes across all sports; female athletes remain underrepresented in several performance domains (§18.2). Individual-response analysis is conceptual and not resistance-training-exclusive.
modules.coach_judgment: how much individualization the environment can sustain and still deliver well; sex-based individual modification on individual grounds (CJ-22).

lessons.title: The variables that matter
lessons.content: Training age, maturation, current capacity, technical competency, schedule, sport exposure, injury and training history, availability, response trend.

lessons.title: Individualization versus customization
lessons.content: The environment as a real constraint: what a coach can deliver well is part of what is appropriate.

lessons.title: When the same program is the right answer
lessons.content: Shared demand, shared training age, shared schedule — and what still gets adjusted at the athlete level.

lessons.title: Why responses look different than they are
lessons.content: Reliability, dose, adherence, outcome choice, time. Four of the five are the coach's before they are the athlete's.

lessons.title: Preference and adherence
lessons.content: A legitimate tiebreaker between similarly appropriate methods, and not a substitute for a target.

lessons.title: Sex as a modifier, not a category
lessons.content: What the evidence supports, what remains uneven, and why no female-specific G3 system exists (§18.2).

lessons.title: The nonresponder conversation
lessons.content: What the label would require, what to say instead, and what to check first.

modules.coaching_applications: Applied to G3 group programming. The module's product is a working practice: one program per shared demand, with a named list of what is adjusted individually and why.

common_errors_claim_audit.text: Customization mistaken for care · complexity the environment cannot deliver · nonresponder labeling after one block (CA-28) · a sex-based programming rule (CJ-22) · individualizing on variables that do not change any decision · ignoring adherence as a determinant of exposure.

knowledge_assessment.item: Which variables are decision-relevant for individualization?
"Two athletes on the same program are not being individualized."
Order what a coach checks before concluding an athlete did not respond.
Athlete preference is best used to…
State G3's position on female-athlete programming in one sentence.

applied_assessment.title: Individualization map
applied_assessment.description: For one real G3 group, the shared program stated, the individually adjusted elements listed with reasons, and the variables deliberately not individualized with reasons.
applied_assessment.standard: shared elements justified; adjustments tied to decision-relevant variables; deliverability in the actual environment addressed; no sex-based rule.

Prerequisite: PS-1 recorded (hard gate) and M4 at standard. Unlocks: M6.

modules.title: Variation, Periodization & Historical Models
modules.framing_statement: Coaches will meet every one of these models in their careers. The purpose of this module is that they meet them already knowing what class of thing they are.
modules.purpose: To establish purposeful variation, to state honestly what the periodization evidence does and does not show, and to classify ten influential frameworks as Class E without dismissing them.

learning_objectives.objective: Define variation as purposeful change and state the four problems it can solve.
State what the volume-equated periodization evidence found — and did not.
Explain why no named periodization model is established as universally superior.
Explain why stability long enough to coach and evaluate is a programming asset.
Identify and correctly classify ten historical and practitioner frameworks.
For any framework, state its contribution, its useful function, and its common overextension.
Explain why "muscle confusion" is not a mechanism.

evidence_classifications.statement: Planned variation can modify volume, intensity, exercise selection, frequency, emphasis, or complexity, and may help manage fatigue, maintain relevance, distribute exposure, address seasonal priorities, or improve adherence
In volume-equated synthesis, periodized training had an advantage for maximal strength over non-periodized training
Hypertrophy superiority for periodized training was not clearly established
Linear and undulating approaches did not show a consistent difference in strength or hypertrophy
Keep a structure stable long enough to coach, load, and evaluate it
"Every athlete needs periodization"
evidence_classifications.class: B / Probable, not absolute — planned variation can help; formality and model depend on context

evidence_classifications.statement: "One periodization model is universally superior"
"Muscle confusion," constant rotation, and novelty for its own sake
GAS, supercompensation, fitness-fatigue, Matveyev, block, Dynamic Correspondence, Bondarchuk, Bompa traditions, LTAD, high/low

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: the periodization evidence is concentrated in adults with varying training histories; direct translation to youth or to a team season is limited. Historical frameworks are represented through modern verified reviews rather than original-language primary texts (§20.3).
modules.coach_judgment: whether to organize formally at all (CJ-07); how much variation before stability and evaluation are lost; how long a structure runs (CJ-19).

lessons.title: What variation is for
lessons.content: Four problems it solves — fatigue management, task relevance, exposure distribution, changing priorities — and one it does not: boredom.

lessons.title: The periodization evidence, stated exactly
lessons.content: Advantage for maximal strength in volume-equated synthesis; hypertrophy unclear; linear versus undulating not consistently different. All three sentences, always together.

lessons.title: Why no model wins
lessons.content: Definitions, volume equating, duration, and testing all vary between studies; "periodization" is not one intervention.

lessons.title: The cost of rotation
lessons.content: A program changed before it can be coached, loaded, and evaluated has produced no information about anything.

lessons.title: Ten frameworks, correctly classified
lessons.content: The full §17.4 table worked through, with the coach practicing the Class E sentence on each.

lessons.title: Where each one gets overextended
lessons.content: GAS as a prescription; supercompensation as a schedule; blocks as universally superior; LTAD stages as fixed ages; high/low as a law.

lessons.title: "Muscle confusion
lessons.content: Why it is not a construct, and why the correction must not become "never change anything."

modules.coaching_applications: Applied to how G3 talks about its own programming. G3 may organize training deliberately and say so; G3 may not present an organization as evidence of superiority, or a named system as validated.

common_errors_claim_audit.text: More variation prevents plateaus (CA-15) · muscle confusion (CA-16) · every athlete requires formal periodization (CA-21) · one model universally superior (CA-22) · supercompensation used as a timetable (CA-18) · a Class E framework presented as validated programming · inverting the correction into "planning doesn't matter."

knowledge_assessment.item: The volume-equated periodization synthesis found…
Match six frameworks to their common overextension.
"Undulating periodization is superior to linear."
State the G3 Class E sentence.
A G3 draft describes a named model as evidence-based programming.

applied_assessment.title: Framework audit
applied_assessment.description: Four frameworks the coach has personally used or been taught, each with its contribution, its useful function, its evidence status, and the specific way the coach has seen it overextended.
applied_assessment.standard: all four correctly classified; no framework presented as validated; at least one overextension identified in the coach's own prior practice.

Prerequisite: M5 at standard. Unlocks: M7. Gate: none.

modules.title: Fatigue, Recovery & Readiness
modules.framing_statement: Every coach has made a decision from a number on a screen or a feeling in an athlete's legs. This module is about making that decision on purpose.
modules.purpose: To separate fatigue, soreness, recovery, and adaptation; to remove the fixed recovery clock without replacing it with a different one; and to establish readiness as a triangulated estimate rather than a measurable state.

learning_objectives.objective: Distinguish fatigue, soreness, recovery, and adaptation.
Explain why fatigue does not establish session quality, and why its absence does not establish failure.
Name the factors that influence recovery context.
Explain why no fixed recovery window applies to all athletes.
Define readiness as a contextual estimate and state what it is not.
Triangulate a readiness decision from at least three input types.
Distinguish functional overreaching, nonfunctional overreaching, and overtraining syndrome, and state the coach's role in each.

evidence_classifications.statement: Fatigue is a reduction in capacity or performance that may be acute or accumulated and can occur alongside productive training
Sleep, nutritional adequacy, psychological stress, sport demands, and training load influence recovery and performance context
Using multiple signals — athlete report, performance trend, recent load, schedule, coach observation — supports proportionate adjustment
Athlete-reported measures may relate to subsequent performance or load, but relationships are variable
Fitness-fatigue and supercompensation are useful heuristics for explaining that training creates both adaptation and performance suppression
evidence_classifications.class: D/E / Heuristic — not direct measurement systems

evidence_classifications.statement: Soreness, fatigue, a fixed 48/72-hour rule, or a readiness score can precisely determine recovery status or today's prescription
Fatigue proves the session was productive
Functional overreaching, nonfunctional overreaching, and overtraining syndrome are interchangeable
evidence_classifications.class: F / Known against claim — OTS requires broader assessment and exclusion of other conditions

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: readiness and self-report evidence comes substantially from elite and professional or team-sport settings, not developmental athletes; thresholds and expectations may not be imported into a scholastic environment (§18.3). Much of the monitoring literature is adult.
modules.coach_judgment: fixed recovery windows (CJ-04) · readiness thresholds (CJ-11) · wellness thresholds (CJ-12) · which readiness signals are credible enough to change a session, and by how much.

lessons.title: Four words that are not synonyms
lessons.content: Fatigue · soreness · recovery · adaptation, each defined against the others.

lessons.title: What fatigue is evidence of
lessons.content: Exposure and tolerance — real information, wrongly used as a scoreboard.

lessons.title: The recovery context
lessons.content: Sleep, nutrition, psychological stress, sport demand, training load, time. Most of it is outside the session.

lessons.title: Killing the clock without replacing it
lessons.content: Why 48/72 fails, and what deliberate spacing looks like without a number.

lessons.title: Readiness, honestly defined
lessons.content: A contextual estimate, not a state; what a "readiness score" actually is; why a single score cannot carry a decision.

lessons.title: Triangulation in practice
lessons.content: Athlete report + recent exposure + schedule + performance trend + observation, and the AS-101-07 three-input minimum as a G3 standard, not a finding.

lessons.title: Overreaching, OTS, and the referral line
lessons.content: Three different things; the coach monitors, communicates, and refers rather than diagnosing (D101-21).

modules.coaching_applications: Applied to the daily adjustment conversation. The module's product is the G3 adjustment sentence: what was seen, from which inputs, what was chosen — maintain, progress, regress, redistribute, or refer — and what would change it.

common_errors_claim_audit.text: No pain, no gain (CA-01) · soreness means it worked (CA-02) · fatigue proves productivity (CA-19) · fixed 48/72-hour recovery (CA-17) · supercompensation as a schedule (CA-18) · a readiness score deciding the session (CA-26) · coach diagnosis of overtraining syndrome (D101-21) · replacing the fixed clock with a different fixed clock.

modules.case_scenario: Case 3 — The athlete is sore. See §10.3. Case 6 — The readiness score is red. See §10.6.

knowledge_assessment.item: Match fatigue, soreness, recovery, and adaptation to what each tells a coach.
"If they're not sore, it wasn't hard enough."
An athlete reports poor sleep and a heavy academic week; recent exposure is moderate; performance trend is stable. What is the decision, and on what basis?
Which inputs count toward the AS-101-07 minimum?
State the difference between nonfunctional overreaching and overtraining syndrome, and the coach's role.

applied_assessment.title: Readiness and adjustment log
applied_assessment.description: Five real adjustment decisions over the practical window, each recording the inputs used, the interpretation, the decision, and what would have changed it.
applied_assessment.standard: at least three input types per decision; no single-metric decision; at least one decision to not adjust, with reasoning; referral considered where indicated.

modules.practical_sign_off_linkage: PS-2 — Readiness & Adjustment Decision. See §14.3. PS-2 gates M8.

modules.title: Concurrent Training & Integrated Demands
modules.framing_statement: "Cardio kills gains" is wrong. "Conditioning never costs anything" is also wrong. This module is about living in the space between them.
modules.purpose: To establish concurrent development as feasible and interference as conditional — with the conditions named, and no separation rule invented.

learning_objectives.objective: Explain that strength and endurance can be developed concurrently.
Name the conditions under which interference becomes practically meaningful.
State which outcomes appear more vulnerable and which less.
Explain why no universal separation interval, sequence, or modality rule exists.
Account for total sport load, not only prescribed conditioning.
Explain why "cardio kills gains" fails as a claim.
State the population limits of the concurrent-training evidence.

evidence_classifications.statement: Concurrent training can improve endurance and resistance-training outcomes simultaneously
Blanket exclusion of conditioning is unsupported
A systematic review reported small interference for lower-body strength adaptations in males but not females, with variation by training status and other moderators
Explosive strength/power and muscle-fiber hypertrophy may be more vulnerable than maximal strength or whole-muscle hypertrophy
Running may be more problematic than cycling for some outcomes
Interference becomes more meaningful with high endurance volume alongside strength/power priorities, closely coupled sessions, high running and impact demand, or poor fatigue management
A single separation interval, sequence, or modality rule applies universally
"Cardio kills strength and muscle gains"

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: concurrent-training research is largely adult and may not represent the practice density, competition schedules, maturation, or sport demands of scholastic athletes. Sex and training-status effects are not consistently represented across sport settings (§18.2, §18.3). One landmark synthesis in this area uses older methods and studies.
modules.coach_judgment: exact separation interval (CJ-08) · session order (CJ-09) · how conditioning is placed around strength and power work in a specific microcycle.

lessons.title: What concurrent training is, and what the argument is actually about
lessons.content: Not whether both can improve — they can — but at what cost, to which outcome.

lessons.title: The moderators
lessons.content: Outcome · modality · dose · training status · sequencing · proximity · recovery resources. Seven, and none of them is a number.

lessons.title: Which outcomes are vulnerable
lessons.content: Explosive strength, power, and fiber hypertrophy versus maximal strength and whole-muscle hypertrophy — stated with its evidence class.

lessons.title: Sport load is conditioning
lessons.content: The practice, the game, the tournament weekend. Counted before any prescribed conditioning is added.

lessons.title: Why no separation rule exists
lessons.content: What such a rule would require, and what varies between the studies that would have to supply it.

lessons.title: "Cardio kills gains," dismantled
lessons.content: The grain of truth, the overreach, and the inversion to avoid.

lessons.title: Placing conditioning in a real week
lessons.content: Worked examples, labeled as examples, with the trade-off in each stated explicitly.

modules.coaching_applications: Applied to G3 weekly planning: total high-demand exposure counted across sport and training before conditioning is prescribed. Nothing is published as a rule; the counting is the standard.

common_errors_claim_audit.text: Cardio kills gains (CA-10) · conditioning treated as categorically harmful · a separation interval quoted as a rule (CJ-08) · sport practice omitted from the load count · inverting the correction into "conditioning is always free" · applying adult concurrent findings to a scholastic athlete without disclosure.

knowledge_assessment.item: Which moderate concurrent-training interference?
Which outcome appears most vulnerable to interference?
"Strength and endurance sessions must be separated by at least six hours."
A team practices five days weekly with high running volume and wants a power emphasis. What changes, and why?
State the population limit of the concurrent-training evidence.

applied_assessment.title: Integrated week
applied_assessment.description: One real athlete or team week with all high-demand exposure counted — sport included — the priority named, the conditioning placement justified, and the trade-off stated.
applied_assessment.standard: sport load counted; priority named; no separation rule asserted; trade-off explicit; population-transfer disclosure present where adult evidence is used.
