modules.title: Youth Athletic Development
modules.framing_statement: The two errors are symmetrical and equally common: the coach who will not load a competent 13-year-old, and the coach who gives that 13-year-old a college program.
modules.purpose: To establish supervised youth training as supported, to remove age and puberty gates without licensing adult dosing, and to make training age the operative variable.

learning_objectives.objective: Distinguish training age, chronological age, and biological maturation.
State what the youth resistance-training evidence supports.
State what it does not license.
Explain why age and puberty gates are unsupported.
Progress a youth athlete by competence, exposure, supervision, and task demand.
Explain the supervision condition and why it is not optional.
State G3's position on early specialization.

evidence_classifications.statement: Supervised, developmentally appropriate resistance training is supported for youth and does not require a fixed chronological age or puberty threshold
Position statements and systematic reviews support youth resistance training when qualified instruction, supervision, sensible progression, and appropriate technique are present
Youth can train strength, power, sprinting, and plyometric qualities when task demands are scaled to competency and context
Adolescent meta-analyses report improvements in jump, sprint, COD, and explosive-strength outcomes with plyometric training
Training age is exposure and competency history, not chronological age; maturation and prior training can be more decision-relevant than age
Novice/intermediate/advanced labels are useful shorthand; no universal evidence-based cut points classify every athlete
Early stages should emphasize supervised technical learning, broad exposure, and manageable progression
Lifting stunts growth · a specific age must be reached first · bodyweight only · youth cannot train power · puberty must precede meaningful preparation
Broad claims that all athletes must specialize early, or that multisport participation is always superior
evidence_classifications.class: F / Overstated — exceeds the evidence in this pack

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: youth age threshold (CJ-16) · puberty (CJ-17) · what counts as "heavy" for a youth athlete (CJ-18) · specialization advice (CJ-21) · how task demands are scaled to competence, maturity, exposure, and supervision.
modules.coach_judgment: youth age threshold (CJ-16) · puberty (CJ-17) · what counts as "heavy" for a youth athlete (CJ-18) · specialization advice (CJ-21) · how task demands are scaled to competence, maturity, exposure, and supervision.

lessons.title: Three ages
lessons.content: Chronological, biological, training — and which one actually predicts what an athlete can be asked to do.

lessons.title: What the evidence supports
lessons.content: Position statements and reviews, stated with their conditions attached every time: qualified instruction, supervision, sensible progression, appropriate technique.

lessons.title: What it does not license
lessons.content: Unsupervised lifting, arbitrary heavy loading, adult volume, progression beyond technical and psychological readiness. Taught immediately after L9.2, never separated from it.

lessons.title: The gates, removed
lessons.content: Age, puberty, bodyweight-only, and the growth-plate claim — each corrected, none replaced with a new number.

lessons.title: The underloading failure
lessons.content: The coach who never progresses a competent, well-supervised youth athlete has made an error of the same class as the coach who overloads one.

lessons.title: Supervision as the condition
lessons.content: Why the ratio, competence, and attention are part of the claim rather than context around it — and how it is documented (AS-101-11).

lessons.title: Specialization, and the parent conversation
lessons.content: What the evidence supports, what it does not, and how to say so to a family that has been told otherwise.

modules.coaching_applications: Applied directly to G3 Youth. Every youth group carries a documented supervision ratio, and every youth progression names competence and exposure rather than age.

common_errors_claim_audit.text: Youth lifting stunts growth (CA-11) · youth should not lift heavy (CA-12) · youth should not train power (CA-13) · athletes must specialize early (CA-14) · an age or puberty gate applied (CJ-16, CJ-17) · adult prescriptions transferred to a middle-school athlete · indefinite underloading justified as caution · supervision omitted from the safety claim.

knowledge_assessment.item: Which variable is most decision-relevant for youth training readiness?
"Youth should not lift heavy."
Which conditions accompany the youth resistance-training evidence?
A 12-year-old with two years of supervised training and a 14-year-old with none. What differs, and why?
State what youth evidence does not license.

applied_assessment.title: Youth progression plan
applied_assessment.description: One real youth athlete or group: entry criteria by competence and exposure, the progression ladder, supervision documented, stop and modify criteria, and the parent-facing explanation.
applied_assessment.standard: no age or puberty gate; no adult dose imported; supervision documented; progression present — a plan that never progresses fails; parent explanation makes no injury-prevention guarantee.

modules.title: Movement Quality, Technique & Coaching Feedback
modules.framing_statement: There is a version of "everyone moves differently" that is coaching, and a version that is an excuse. This module draws the line where the task is.
modules.purpose: To establish task-relevant technical standards that permit legitimate individual variation, to teach feedback as a purposeful tool, and to remove screening and asymmetry from the injury-prediction business without discarding what they describe.

learning_objectives.objective: Explain why technique matters for effectiveness, progression, and risk management.
Define task-relevant technical constraints for a foundational task.
Explain what produces legitimate movement variation.
Distinguish legitimate variation from an uncoached movement problem.
Use feedback purposefully — form, timing, frequency — rather than constantly.
State what a movement screen describes and what it does not predict.
State why asymmetry is not automatically pathology.

evidence_classifications.statement: Technique matters for task effectiveness, progression, and risk management
Research does not establish one universally "perfect" movement solution for all athletes
Anthropometry, injury history, task goal, equipment, and individual coordination can produce legitimate movement variation
Coaches should establish task-relevant setup, intent, execution constraints, and progression criteria, with demonstration, concise cues, and appropriate feedback
Augmented feedback can improve motor learning and acute resistance-training performance
Feedback effectiveness depends on form, timing, frequency, and athlete/task context; constant immediate correction is not automatically optimal
Acute performance improvements from feedback equal long-term sport transfer
Movement-screen composite scores predict subsequent injury
evidence_classifications.class: F / Known against standalone claim — screening evidence is inconsistent or insufficient for injury prediction

evidence_classifications.statement: Asymmetry automatically predicts injury
evidence_classifications.class: F / Overstated — requires task and context interpretation; no universal predictive threshold established

evidence_classifications.statement: A universal movement-screen score, one asymmetry threshold, or one technique template can predict injury or dictate one correct solution
Every athlete needs identical movement standards

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: movement-screen and injury-prediction studies use inconsistent injury definitions and varied samples, including one single-setting collegiate cohort; screening results should not be generalized to an individual athlete's causal injury risk. Feedback and motor-learning evidence spans diverse populations and tasks (§18.3).
modules.coach_judgment: movement-screen cutoffs (CJ-14) · asymmetry thresholds (CJ-15) · technique templates (CJ-20) · what an observed movement means for this athlete and this task.

lessons.title: Why technique matters
lessons.content: Effectiveness, progression, and risk management — three distinct reasons, often conflated into a vague appeal to safety.

lessons.title: Constraints, not templates
lessons.content: Defining setup, intent, execution constraints, and progression criteria for a foundational task, and letting the rest vary.

lessons.title: What produces legitimate variation
lessons.content: Anthropometry, history, task goal, equipment, coordination — and how a coach tells this from a coaching gap.

lessons.title: Feedback that teaches
lessons.content: Form, timing, frequency; why constant correction is not automatically better; why the acute effect is not the learning.

lessons.title: What a screen describes
lessons.content: A performance of a task, under a protocol, on a day. Useful description; not prediction.

lessons.title: Asymmetry without alarm
lessons.content: Task- and context-dependent; measurement reliability first; no universal threshold — and no substitute threshold invented.

lessons.title: The conversation after a screen
lessons.content: What can honestly be said to an athlete, a parent, and a sport coach — and where the referral line sits (D101-21).

modules.coaching_applications: Applied to how G3 coaches a foundational task on the floor. The module's product is a written constraint set the coach can actually cue from, and a list of the variations they will accept without correcting.

common_errors_claim_audit.text: Every athlete needs identical standards (CA-09) · movement screens predict injury (CA-23) · asymmetry predicts injury (CA-24) · a technique template applied universally (CJ-20) · "everyone moves differently" used to avoid coaching · constant correction mistaken for good coaching · an acute feedback effect reported as learning · a screen result communicated as a risk verdict.

knowledge_assessment.item: A movement screen result is best described as…
"Asymmetry above a threshold requires corrective work."
Which produce legitimate movement variation?
Two athletes perform a task differently; one is a legitimate variation, one is not. Distinguish them and justify.
State what a coach may honestly tell a parent after a screen.

applied_assessment.title: Constraint set and feedback plan
applied_assessment.description: For one foundational task: the task-relevant constraints, the acceptable variations, the cues, the feedback plan including frequency and timing, and the stop/modify criteria.
applied_assessment.standard: constraints tied to the task rather than to an aesthetic; acceptable variation stated explicitly; feedback plan not constant; no injury-prediction language.

modules.title: Training Load, Testing & Monitoring
modules.framing_statement: This module is taught after the coach can already coach, deliberately. A measurement in the hands of someone who cannot coach the athlete is a number looking for a decision.
modules.purpose: To establish what load, testing, and monitoring data can and cannot support — validity, reliability, error, standardization — and to remove ACWR, wellness, and readiness scores from the prediction business.

learning_objectives.objective: Distinguish external and internal training load and state what each answers.
Explain why no single load metric captures total training effect.
Define validity, reliability, sensitivity, typical error, familiarization, and standardization.
Explain why a test can be valid for one construct and not another.
Interpret a test change against measurement error and decision consequence.
State what the ACWR evidence supports and what it does not.
Explain why technology does not create validity.

evidence_classifications.statement: External load describes completed work; internal load describes athlete response; neither alone captures the entire training effect or injury risk
Session RPE, volume load, GPS/wearables, heart rate, and wellness questionnaires can be useful monitoring inputs when standardized and interpreted with context
Monitoring measures are not direct measures of tissue state, adaptation, or injury causation
A test can be valid for one construct and not another; a reliable test is required to detect small meaningful change; standardization and familiarization reduce avoidable noise
Prefer repeated within-athlete baselines and context-consistent testing over uncritical normative comparison
Smallest worthwhile change is conceptually useful, but its calculation and practical threshold depend on context, reliability, and decision use — not a universal cut point
ACWR shows associations with injury outcomes in some populations
High heterogeneity, calculation choices, statistical concerns, and contextual differences prevent ACWR use as a universal injury-prediction law or standalone decision rule
ACWR precisely predicts injury, or a fixed "safe zone" automatically prevents it
Athlete-reported measures relate to subsequent performance or load, variably
A readiness score automatically determines today's training
Technology makes programming more scientific

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: load-monitoring and readiness evidence is drawn substantially from elite, professional, and team-sport settings with data consistency a scholastic environment usually cannot match; ACWR samples are dominated by team-sport, soccer, adult, and professional cohorts, with youth settings less certain. Thresholds may not be imported (§18.3). The most recent ACWR meta-analysis is flagged for downstream risk-of-bias review (§20.1).
modules.coach_judgment: readiness thresholds (CJ-11) · wellness thresholds (CJ-12) · ACWR safe zones (CJ-13) · whether a given metric is worth collecting at all in this environment.

lessons.title: Two questions, two loads
lessons.content: What was done, and what it cost this athlete. Different questions, different metrics, neither sufficient.

lessons.title: The measurement vocabulary
lessons.content: Validity, reliability, sensitivity, typical error, familiarization, standardization — defined operationally, with a worked example for each.

lessons.title: Valid for what
lessons.content: The construct question, applied to four tests coaches actually run.

lessons.title: Change versus noise
lessons.content: Interpreting a small improvement against typical error, baseline variability, and the cost of being wrong — the M11 core skill.

lessons.title: ACWR, stated exactly
lessons.content: Associations in some datasets; heterogeneity, calculation choices, and statistical concerns; one contextual input, never a rule (§19.5).

lessons.title: Readiness and wellness data
lessons.content: What a self-report score is, what it associates with, and why triangulation (AS-101-07) is the only defensible use.

lessons.title: Technology and the actionable question
lessons.content: AS-101-14 in practice: the question, the reliability, and the possible responses — all defined before collection.

modules.coaching_applications: Applied to G3's own monitoring practice. The module's product is a short, defensible metric set: what G3 collects, why, how it is standardized, and what decision each could change. Anything that survives none of those questions is not collected.

common_errors_claim_audit.text: ACWR predicts injury (CA-25) · a readiness score decides the session (CA-26) · technology makes programming scientific (CA-27) · a 2% change treated as real · normative comparison replacing an athlete's own baseline · collecting a metric with no decision attached · a construct-mismatched test used as evidence · a monitoring output described as a diagnosis (D101-17).

modules.case_scenario: Case 7 — The ACWR "danger zone." See §10.7. Case 9 — The test improves 2%. See §10.9.

A monitoring report states that a wearable output shows an athlete is not recovered.

applied_assessment.description: The coach's own proposed metric set: for each, the question it answers, its reliability limits, its standardization, the decisions it could change, and what would cause G3 to stop collecting it.
applied_assessment.standard: every metric carries a question and a possible response; at least one metric eliminated with reasoning; no threshold asserted; change interpreted against error.

modules.title: Evidence-Based Coaching, Scope & the G3 Decision System
modules.framing_statement: Everything in the first eleven modules exists so that this one can be short. The coach already knows the distinctions; this module makes them run the loop out loud, and stop when they should.
modules.purpose: To integrate the nine-step loop, install the three-layer reasoning model as a spoken habit, and establish scope of practice as a coaching competence rather than a disclaimer.

learning_objectives.objective: Define evidence-based coaching as integration rather than deference in either direction.
Identify which of the three layers any statement belongs to.
Explain why perception evidence is not effectiveness evidence.
Run the nine-step loop on a real athlete, out loud.
State the boundaries of performance-coaching scope.
Recognize and act on a referral trigger.
Communicate uncertainty to an athlete, parent, or sport coach without losing authority.

evidence_classifications.statement: Evidence-based practice integrates best available research with coach expertise, athlete values and preferences, and environmental constraints
It is neither "research says, therefore everyone must" nor "experience overrides research"
Practitioners, coaches, and athletes value research-informed practice while also valuing sport knowledge, experience, and communication
evidence_classifications.class: B / Probable — perception evidence, not evidence that any individual practice is effective

evidence_classifications.statement: Use evidence to set plausible boundaries and compare options; use professional judgment to adapt within those boundaries
evidence_classifications.basis: EP101-01, EP101-02 — governance records; this is a statement about G3 practice, carried at the class the Evidence Pack assigns

evidence_classifications.statement: Performance coaches should manage exposure, technique, progressions, observation, and communication, and should not diagnose, clear return to sport, or prescribe rehabilitation beyond scope
Functional overreaching, nonfunctional overreaching, and overtraining syndrome are not interchangeable; OTS requires broader assessment and exclusion of other conditions
The G3 three-layer model — Evidence / G3 Applied Standard / Coach Judgment

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: the evidence-based-practice survey evidence comes from an Australian professional-sport context and reports perceptions rather than outcomes; it is not generalized to G3's scholastic environment as evidence of what works.
modules.coach_judgment: how much evidence is enough to act in a given situation; how uncertainty is communicated to this athlete and this family.

lessons.title: Evidence-based coaching, correctly defined
lessons.content: Four inputs, integrated. The two failure modes named — the slogan and the anecdote — and why both feel like rigor.

lessons.title: The three layers
lessons.content: Evidence · G3 Applied Standard · Coach Judgment (§21.3). Coaches sort thirty real statements into the three, and the exercise is timed.

lessons.title: Perception is not effectiveness
lessons.content: Why the survey finding is interesting and why it proves nothing about any method.

lessons.title: Running the loop out loud
lessons.content: The nine steps applied to a real athlete the coach brings, narrated for a peer.

lessons.title: Scope, defined by what the coach does
lessons.content: Exposure, technique, progression, observation, communication — and the four categories that sit outside.

lessons.title: Referral triggers and the handoff
lessons.content: What is said, what is documented, what training continues, and why referral is not abandonment.

lessons.title: Saying "I don't know" with authority
lessons.content: The sentence forms for uncertainty (Appendix D), rehearsed against an athlete, a parent, and a sport coach.

modules.coaching_applications: Applied to every subsequent G3 conversation. The three-layer habit is the single most portable output of this course, and it is the thing G3 102 through G3 105 assume from the first page.

common_errors_claim_audit.text: "The research says" used to end a conversation (§3.1) · experience used to override stronger evidence (D101-20) · perception evidence cited as effectiveness (EP101-40 limitation) · an Applied Standard presented as a finding (§7.17) · coach diagnosis of a medical condition (D101-21) · referral used to avoid a hard conversation · uncertainty communicated as incompetence.

cases.title: "Progressive Overload Means More Weight"
cases.situation: Marcus, 16, has been in the G3 program for seven months. His main lift has not moved in five weeks. His technique degrades noticeably in the last two reps of every working set, he plays a fall sport with four practices a week, and he reports sleeping about six hours on school nights. His previous coach's rule was to add five pounds every session, and Marcus asks why that has stopped happening.
cases.decision_required: What progresses, what does not, and what do you tell Marcus?
cases.defensible_variation: A coach who progresses volume with a technical constraint attached passes. A coach who holds everything for two weeks to address sleep and sport load, and says so, also passes. A coach who progresses load with a reduced rep target and a stated technical criterion passes if the reasoning is explicit.
cases.failure_modes: Adding load anyway · publishing a replacement rule · declaring the athlete a nonresponder (CA-28) · progressing the variable the coach prefers to coach rather than the one that serves the target · never progressing anything and calling it caution · omitting sport load and sleep from the analysis.

cases.title: The Sport-Looking Exercise
cases.situation: A visiting coach runs your baseball group through single-leg medicine-ball rotational throws on a BOSU, explaining that it is the most sport-specific exercise available because it looks like a swing and challenges stability the way the field does. Your athletes like it. The head coach asks your opinion.
cases.decision_required: What do you say, and what do you do with the exercise?
cases.defensible_variation: A coach who keeps it, labeled as general or coordination work with a stated cost, passes. A coach who removes it because the week cannot afford it and says why, passes. A coach who keeps it and claims swing transfer fails.
cases.failure_modes: Accepting the resemblance claim (CA-07) · accepting the instability claim (CA-08) · inverting into "instability is worthless" · declaring specificity without naming a dimension · ignoring the opportunity cost · avoiding the conversation because the head coach asked.

cases.title: The Athlete Is Sore
cases.situation: Two athletes, same session, three days ago. Athlete A is still sore and says it was the best workout they have had in months. Athlete B is not sore at all and asks whether they should be doing more. Both are on the same program, in week three of a block.
cases.decision_required: What does the soreness tell you about each athlete, and what changes?
cases.defensible_variation: A coach who reduces Athlete A's session today after triangulating passes. A coach who runs both as planned and explains why passes. A coach who adds work for Athlete B because they are not sore fails.
cases.failure_modes: Soreness read as effectiveness (CA-02) · absence of soreness read as failure · fatigue read as productivity (CA-19) · changing the block on either athlete's report (CA-15) · adding volume to chase soreness (CA-03) · no defined outcome ever named.

cases.title: "Cardio Kills Gains"
cases.situation: A high-school football staff has removed all conditioning from the off-season because a strength coach told them cardio kills gains. The athletes report poorly to camp. The head coach now wants "as much conditioning as possible" added back, three days a week, running, immediately before lifting.
cases.decision_required: What goes in the week, and what do you tell the staff?
cases.defensible_variation: A coach who separates the modalities within the day and says what it costs passes. A coach who uses lower-impact modality for part of the volume and explains why passes. A coach who keeps running before lifting for a specific stated reason, having named the cost to the power priority, passes.
cases.failure_modes: Endorsing either absolute (CA-10) · quoting a separation interval as a rule · omitting sport load · treating all conditioning as one thing · applying adult findings without disclosure · refusing to give the staff an answer.

cases.title: The Middle-School Athlete
cases.situation: Ellie, 12, joins a G3 Youth group of sixteen with one coach. No structured training history, coordinated, attentive, no injury history. Her father has been told by another coach that she should not lift until she is fifteen, should not lift heavy until after puberty, and should stick to bodyweight until then. He asks what G3 will do differently and why.
cases.decision_required: What does Ellie's program consist of, how does it progress, and what do you tell her father?
cases.defensible_variation: A coach who introduces external load once competence is demonstrated, with a stated criterion, passes. A coach who stays with bodyweight and implement work for the first block and says exactly what would change it also passes.
cases.failure_modes: Accepting any gate (CA-11, CA-12, CA-13) · substituting a different threshold · importing adult volume · complexity beyond the supervision ratio · promising injury prevention · never progressing · dismissing the other coach rather than explaining the evidence.

cases.title: The Readiness Score Is Red
cases.situation: Your facility has begun using a wellness app. This morning it shows red for Priya, a collegiate athlete, with a recovery score of 31. She says she feels fine, slept normally, and has a conference match in four days. Her recent training load has been moderate. Her last two performance markers were stable. The app recommends a rest day.
cases.defensible_variation: A coach who proceeds as planned while watching warm-up quality closely passes. A coach who reduces intensity modestly with the match in mind — a schedule decision, not a score decision — passes if the reasoning is stated. A coach who cancels the session on the score alone fails.
cases.failure_modes: Automatic cancellation (CA-26) · dismissing the app entirely rather than weighting it · treating the score as a measurement (§2.4) · no reliability question asked · the decision made from the phone rather than the room · a new threshold invented.

cases.title: The ACWR "Danger Zone"
cases.situation: A sport coach shares a dashboard showing three of your athletes in an ACWR "danger zone" and asks you to hold them out of the next two sessions. The load data comes from session RPE collected inconsistently over five weeks, with two weeks of missing entries during exams.
cases.decision_required: What do you do, and what do you tell the sport coach?
cases.defensible_variation: A coach who reviews all three athletes individually and adjusts one on other grounds passes. A coach who changes nothing and explains the data-quality problem passes. A coach who holds all three out on the ratio fails.
cases.failure_modes: Treating the zone as a rule (CA-25) · abandoning load monitoring in reaction (D101-17 boundary) · not questioning the data quality · deferring to the sport coach's authority instead of the evidence · inventing a different cutoff · communicating in a way that makes the sport coach an adversary.

cases.title: The Movement-Screen Failure
cases.situation: A new athlete scores poorly on a movement screen your facility has used for years. The parent has read that a low score means high injury risk and asks whether their child should be training at all. The athlete has no pain, no injury history, and moves well in the tasks you have actually coached.
cases.decision_required: What does the screen tell you, and what do you tell the parent?
cases.defensible_variation: A coach who addresses one specific observed limitation within normal programming passes. A coach who records the screen and changes nothing, explaining why, passes. A coach who runs a corrective block that displaces the athlete's actual training fails.
cases.failure_modes: Treating the score as a risk verdict (CA-23) · treating asymmetry as pathology (CA-24) · reassuring the parent with the opposite absolute ("screens mean nothing") · a corrective block that displaces training · an unnecessary referral · a threshold invented to replace the one refused.

cases.title: The Test Improves 2%
cases.situation: After a six-week block, a team's mean vertical jump has improved 2%. The typical error for your protocol is approximately 3%. Testing was done at a different time of day than baseline, two athletes were absent, and the head coach wants to know whether the block worked.
cases.decision_required: What can you conclude, and what do you report?
cases.defensible_variation: A coach who re-tests under a standardized protocol before concluding passes. A coach who reports the result as uninterpretable and cites other evidence of the block's effect passes. A coach who reports a 2% improvement as a result fails.
cases.failure_modes: Reporting the change as real · declaring the block a failure on the same data · importing a universal SWC threshold · ignoring the protocol change · ignoring the sample change · never asking what decision the test was meant to inform.

cases.title: "Nonresponder"
cases.situation: After one twelve-week block, one athlete in a group of fourteen shows no improvement in the tested outcome while the rest improved. Their coach concludes they are a nonresponder and wants to move them to a completely different training approach.
cases.decision_required: What do you check, and what do you do?
cases.defensible_variation: A coach who repeats the block with improved adherence tracking passes. A coach who changes the exposure after completing the checks and stating the rationale passes. A coach who adds a second relevant outcome before concluding anything passes.
cases.failure_modes: Applying the label (CA-28) · changing everything without the checks · blaming the athlete · using group mean improvement as the standard for an individual · never revisiting the question · telling the athlete they are a nonresponder.

cases.title: The Periodization Debate
cases.situation: Two coaches on your staff disagree. One insists all G3 programming should be block periodized, citing sequencing and concentrated loading. The other says periodization is marketing and the only thing that matters is progressive overload. Both want you to settle it, and both have cited research.
cases.decision_required: What is G3's position, and how do you settle it?
cases.defensible_variation: A staff that adopts a consistent organizing structure for operational reasons, labeled as such, passes. A staff that programs without formal periodization and can explain their variation logic passes. Either becomes a failure the moment it is defended as evidence-based superiority.
cases.failure_modes: Declaring a model superior (CA-22) · declaring periodization unnecessary for everyone (CA-21 inverted) · citing only the half of the evidence that supports a position · presenting a Class E framework as validated · settling by seniority rather than by layer.

cases.title: Scope of Practice
cases.situation: Mid-session, a 17-year-old athlete mentions that her knee has been "catching" for about three weeks, that it swells after games, and that she has not told her parents or her coach because she does not want to lose her spot. She asks you not to say anything and to just modify her program.
cases.decision_required: What do you do, in what order?
cases.defensible_variation: A coach who speaks with her first and then escalates the same day passes. A coach who involves the athletic trainer immediately and informs the parents through the appropriate channel passes. A coach who documents, escalates, and modifies the session so she is not sitting out entirely passes.
cases.failure_modes: Agreeing to keep it quiet · modifying the program instead of escalating · offering an opinion about what the injury is · clearing her to play · removing her from training entirely as an over-correction · escalating without ever talking to her.

terminal_defense.title: Foundations of Athletic Performance Defense
terminal_defense.format: 20–30 minutes with an approved assessor, using the coach's own athlete or group and their own artifacts. The assessor works the nine obligations (§1.4) in order and probes at least four.
must_defend: youth and development context where relevant
mandatory_probes: What is the demand, what is the target quality, and how would you know the target moved?
Which variable are you progressing, why that one, and what did you set aside?
What is this method expected to transfer to, and what would show you it did not?
Which part of what you just told me is evidence, which is G3 policy, and which is your judgment?
What in this plan do you not know? Say it plainly.
What would make you change this — and what would make you refer?
Tell me what you would say to this athlete's parent about injury risk.
non_compensable_failures: cannot answer probe 4 (evidence vs G3 policy vs judgment)
cannot answer probe 5 (states what is not known)
makes an injury-prevention guarantee on probe 7
cites a threshold, template, or published number as justification
crosses a scope boundary in any answer

assessment_system.design_rule: Applied and coaching competencies are never certified by multiple choice alone. Knowledge is capped at 16%, and no learner may pass with a failing score in Application, Coaching, Evaluation, or Defense regardless of total.
item_writing_standards: No item may be answerable from a single memorized sentence outside the Knowledge band, which is capped at 16%.
Every scenario item commits the learner before feedback.
Distractors are real coaching errors, drawn from the §16 Claim Audit register and the module error lists.

No assessment key may require a conditional, emerging, historical, or practitioner claim to be treated as established science — no key may depend on a Class C, D, or E claim, or on an Unknown certainty rating.
No item key may require a Class F claim to be treated as true. Class F material appears only as the error to be identified.

No item key may require a number G3 has not established — no weekly volume, frequency, intensity, rest interval, recovery window, dose threshold, separation interval, ACWR value, readiness or wellness cut-point, screen cutoff, asymmetry threshold, smallest-worthwhile-change figure, or youth age as a keyed answer.
No item key may treat an acute result as chronic evidence, a model output as a measurement, or an association as a transfer claim (§2.4).
No item key may rest on perception evidence as though it established effectiveness (M12, EP101-40).
Where more than one answer is defensible, the item is a decision item scored on reasoning, not multiple choice with a hidden preference.
Every item carries metadata: module, competency, doctrine, applied standard, evidence class, certainty, level, and key source.

nine_obligations: Define the performance demand. What outcome or quality actually matters here?
Understand the athlete. Training age, chronological age, maturation, capacity, history, schedule, availability, constraints.
Identify the target. What quality is being trained, and why this one?
Select an appropriate exposure. A method capable of producing the intended stimulus — and say what that stimulus is.
Apply sufficient dose. Enough to adapt, without assuming more is better.
Preserve recoverability. It has to fit the athlete's whole life, not just the session.
Measure the response. Reliable, relevant information — never fatigue or soreness as a proxy.
Evaluate transfer. Did the target outcome change, or did only the exercise?
Adjust. Progress, maintain, regress, redistribute, or change — with a stated reason.

binding_rules: No downstream course may loosen an upstream evidence, scope, measurement, or programming-integrity standard.
Where domain courses overlap, the more specific domain governs only inside that domain; otherwise the upstream standard controls.

foundations.taxonomy_rule: U is the machine-readable series class for a question about which no defensible evidence-class assignment can be made. 'Unknown' remains the human-facing certainty label.
